VINTO is somebody else's card game, and this is an unofficial app for it. The game, its rules and the people who made it are at vinto.game.
Who made this app, what else is on the shelf, and how it is put together.

Send the game to a friend. Four seats, and three of them can be bots.
Vinto — the card game of holding less and knowing more. Free, in the browser, no sign-up: %1$s
How hard the three of them think about their move.
How quickly the table plays out what happened. Three bots take their turns between one tap and the next, and this is how long you get to watch them.
The felt is green either way. This is everything around it.

Whether cards fly, or simply appear where they land. Reduced keeps every ring, verdict and pause — the game is still narrated, it just doesn’t move. System follows your device’s accessibility setting.
A card dealt, a card landing, a penalty, the round ending — and nothing else.
A small kick under the thumb when a card is touched, a move lands, or a rule bites.

How many rounds get played, and how long they take. Never your name, your room codes or anything that could point back at you — there is nowhere in what we send to put them. Turning this off sends nothing at all.
There is a round in progress. Forgetting it cannot be undone, and the running score of the session goes with it.
Rounds played, how many you won, your best hand and your streak. Kept on this device only — never sent anywhere.
The table moves on in %1$d s
%1$s is taking a card from the deck
Everyone else plays one hand between them, against yours.
You play the coalition’s hand against %1$s.
One hand between the three of them, against %1$s.
%1$d in the deck — what that means

%1$d cards left to draw from.\n\nWhen it runs out, the discard pile is shuffled back into it and everything anybody had learned from watching that pile stops being worth anything — including what you learned. A round that is nearly out of deck is a round to call Vinto in.
You called Vinto, so your hand was set against the best of the others’.
%1$s called Vinto, so their hand was set against the best of yours.
Nobody called Vinto — the deck ran out, so the round ended and every hand was counted.

Something the table did that it should not have? Send the game with it.\n\nWhat gets sent is the deal it started from, every move since, and a checksum after each one — enough to replay this exact game, here or in the web app, and see the same thing go wrong. No account, no device details, nothing about you.
Everybody may look at two of their own cards before the round starts, once. From here on the game is memory: yours against three other people's.
They turn face down again — remember where they were. Everybody else has peeked at two of theirs as well.
Only name one you have seen
You looked at this card, so you know what it is. Name it right and you play its action for free. Name it wrong and you take a penalty card — so only name one you are sure of.
Anybody holding that rank may throw it in

The moment a card lands face up, everyone gets a chance to be rid of a match — and to use its action. Wrong rank costs you a penalty card and shuts you out of that card — the next one to land is a fresh chance.
Watch what they take and what they put down. That, and the line-by-line under here, is everything you get to know about their hands.
This is the card's own action, and it is free — it costs you nothing to use, and the card goes on the pile afterwards either way.
The new card goes in face down, and the one it replaces goes face up on the pile for everybody to read. Give up the card you least want to be holding — the highest one you know about.

Put it in your hand — face down, in place of a card you own, which goes face up on the pile — or throw it away. Every card in your hand counts against you, so a low one is worth keeping. If it has an action, playing it now instead is the third choice, and it costs you nothing to take.
Two ways to start a turn
From the deck, sight unseen — or off the pile, but only an action card nobody has used, and then you must play it at once rather than keep it.
Every turn starts the same way
A turn begins by taking a card. The deck is face down, so what you get is a surprise — that is the risk you are being paid for.
Every card counts against you and the lowest hand wins. This is a real round against three real opponents — the coach only walks beside you.
Worth exactly what they say and nothing else. Small ones are what a winning hand is made of.
7 and 8 — look at one of yours
Worth 7 and 8, which is a lot to be holding. What you get for it is a look at one of your own cards — and this game is memory, so a card you have seen is worth more to you than a card you have not.
9 and 10 — look at one of theirs
The same look, pointed the other way: one card in somebody else's hand. Remember where it was. Two turns later it is what tells you whether to call.

Worth 10. It swaps two cards belonging to two different players — never two of anybody's own — and nobody looks at either of them first. Good for pushing a card you know is bad into somebody else's hand; a gamble with anything you know is good.
Queen — look at two, then decide
Also worth 10, and the strongest card in the game: look at any two cards from two different players, and only then choose whether to swap them. The Jack gambles. The Queen knows.
King — worth nothing, and does anything

Worth nothing at all, which alone makes it worth keeping. Its action points at any card on the table — yours or anybody's — and names it. Right: that card leaves the hand it was in, and its action becomes yours to play. Wrong: everybody sees what it really was, and you take a penalty card.
What you name is what you get to play

So you are really choosing an action, out of the cards you have seen. Name a 7 or an 8 and you get a look at one of your own. Name a Jack and you get its blind swap — and you pick both cards, which is how a Joker you have spotted comes to you and your worst card goes the other way. Name a Queen and you look at two before deciding whether to trade.

Whoever was holding it, the card you name leaves their hand. Naming your own 10 takes ten points off your total; naming Don's Joker takes his minus one away and leaves him a card worse off. One King, two jobs — which of them matters more is the read.
An Ace is worth 1 and makes whoever you choose draw a penalty card. A Joker is worth minus one — the best card in the deck, and the one never to give away.
Cards come off the deck. What anybody throws away lands face up beside it, where the whole table can read it — including you.
Three bots, each with five cards they can see no better than you can. The plate that lights up green is whoever's turn it is.

It explains the moment you are in and what every card does. The boxed game comes with reminder cards for exactly this, one per player — nobody is expected to hold fourteen ranks in their head, here or at a table.

You, and the two who did not call, are the coalition: one turn each, and only your single best hand is compared with the caller's — so it is a team against one hand. At a real table you would talk it over and pool what you know. Nobody may touch the caller's cards, and the game will not let you try.

At the end of any turn of yours, the gold button is there: press it when you believe your hand is the lowest at the table. It was hidden while you were learning because it ends the round for everybody — from here on it is yours to press, and pressing it early is how most people lose their first game.

A game is rounds, one after another, with those points carried between them, played to a clock somebody agrees beforehand — half an hour is usual. When the time is up the round in progress is finished, and whoever has the most points comes first for 5 game points, second for 3, third for 2. A round won by three counts the same whether you won it by one point or by twenty.

The caller's hand is set against the best hand among everybody else. Lower, and the caller takes +3 while everybody else loses 1 each. Level counts as the caller's: +3 to them, nothing lost by anyone. Beaten, and the caller loses 1 while every one of the others takes +3.
That is the bet that their hand is the lowest at the table. It ends the round: everybody else gets exactly one more turn, and then every hand is turned over.
Your table, not mine — nothing here is a wrong move. The lesson picks up wherever you take it.
A card that breathes can be touched right now.
The chip under the piles names the rank the window is open for.
Every move is written down in this box — glance at it when cards moved faster than you could read.
The green number counts what is left in the deck.
%1$s — worth %2$s, and it does nothing at all. A hand full of small ones of these is a good hand.
Every hand is face up and the round is scored. Every rule you met in here is one a real game plays by — there is no practice version of it.
Watch what they take, and what they put back down.
What the table is telling you
Numbers — worth what they say, and nothing else
Lookers — buy you a card you can remember
Movers — put a card somewhere else

Every card in a hand counts against you, so the lowest total wins. Call Vinto when you think yours is lowest — everybody else then plays one more turn together, and only their best hand is compared to yours.
%1$s. It is worth %2$d. It has no action, so it can only go into your hand or onto the pile.
Look at two of your own cards and remember them — they go face-down again when the round starts. Everything after that is memory.
Every hand is face-up. The lowest total wins the round; the player who called Vinto is scored against the best hand among everybody else.
Anybody holding a card of the same rank may throw it in, which gets it out of their hand for nothing. Get the rank wrong and you take a penalty card, and you cannot toss in again this round.
Vinto has been called. Everybody else plays one last turn as a coalition, and only their best hand counts against the caller's.
Draw from the deck, or take the top of the discard pile if it is an action card nobody has played. Keep what lowers your total; call Vinto when you think yours is the lowest.
Tap one of your cards to say what you think it is.
Table talk — the coalition takes your word for it, right or wrong.
Right plays its action; wrong costs you a card.
A wrong one costs you a penalty card.
You guessed wrong on this card, so you are out of this one. The next card to land is a fresh chance.
You guessed wrong, and in the final round that is the rest of the round.
%1$s called Vinto, so the round was scored against their hand.
The deck ran out, so the round ended and every hand was counted.

%1$s called Vinto. Who plays for the rest of you?

Round over — you finished on %1$d, best was %2$d

Anonymous counts only: how many rounds are played, how far people get, whether a table stalled, and what a room costs to run. Never your name, your room code, what is in your hand, or anything that could be traced back to you or your device — there is nowhere in what is sent to put those. It can be switched off in Settings, and a browser that asks not to be tracked switches it off for you.
A green ring on a seat
Whose turn it is. It flashes as the turn arrives, because three bots can take theirs between one tap and the next.
That player has called Vinto. Nobody may touch their cards for the rest of the round.
A red ring, and a hand that flinches
A penalty card just landed there — a wrong guess, or a wrong toss-in.
The coalition: everybody except the Vinto caller, playing their last turn together against that one hand.
A gold ring on the discard
That card was put down without its action being used, so the next player may take it and play it instead of drawing. A card whose action *was* played has no ring.
It can be touched right now. If nothing breathes, the table is waiting on somebody else.
Cards sweeping back into the deck
The deck ran out, so the pile was shuffled back into it. Everything anybody had learned from watching that pile is now out of date.
A card that lifts towards the middle
Somebody is looking at it. Everyone sees *which* card was looked at — only the player entitled to it sees the face.
